title: ReplicaSet scale-down spreads pod deletions across nodes, preventing efficient node consolidation
body:
## What would you like to be added?

The ReplicaSet controller's pod deletion sort order during scale-down should have an option to concentrate deletions on nodes that are closest to empty, rather than spreading deletions evenly across nodes.

When a Deployment scales down, the RS controller's [sort order](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set_utils.go) preferentially removes pods from nodes that have the most co-located replicas from the same owner. This spreads deletions across nodes. It maintains even replica distribution, but it works against node autoscalers like Karpenter and cluster-autoscaler, which need empty or nearly-empty nodes to reclaim compute with minimal additional pod disruption.

**Example:**

5 nodes, each running 4 pods from one Deployment (20 replicas total). HPA scales down to 10.

| | Today (spreading) | With consolidation-aware deletion |
|---|---|---|
| Pods removed per node | 2, 2, 2, 2, 2 | 4, 4, 2, 0, 0 |
| Empty nodes after scale-down | 0 | 2 |
| Additional evictions needed | Yes, autoscaler must evict more pods to consolidate | None, 2 nodes can be removed immediately |
| Total pod disruptions | 10 (scale-down) + N (consolidation) | 10 (scale-down only) |

The same 10 pods are deleted in both cases. The difference is *which* pods. Concentrating deletions on fewer nodes produces empty nodes that the autoscaler can remove without additional disruption.

**Proposed approach:** A feature-gated change to the RS controller's pod deletion sort order that prefers pods on nodes with fewer total active pods (consolidation-friendly), as an alternative to the current spreading behavior. This is tracked in [kubernetes/enhancements#5982](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5982).

This issue is part of a broader discussion on coordinating workload scale-in with node autoscaling. See the [community discussion document](https://docs.google.com/document/d/193Fx7and-DitsGG1ly9-r1f26wmux5gMG8N3G-jPjZU/) and the [Node Lifecycle Management use cases document](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1EINvuVzEoRra0CKH6uQnOcQJVbd7ZnxT1bcyySN-r7c/) (use case 5) for the full context.

**Related work:**
- [kubernetes/enhancements#5982](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5982): KEP for RS controller consolidation heuristic, currently on-hold
- [#107598](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/107598): Configurable down-scaling behaviour in ReplicaSets (closed, predecessor proposal)
- [#123541](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/123541): Extend scale subresource to support pod-deletion-cost (closed, predecessor proposal)
- [KEP-2255](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/2255): Pod Deletion Cost (existing annotation mechanism)
- [Karpenter Pod Deletion Cost Controller RFC](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/karpenter/pull/2935): Autoscaler-side approach using annotations

## Why is this needed?

The ReplicaSet controller and node autoscalers optimize for different goals independently. The RS controller spreads pod deletions to maintain even distribution. The autoscaler needs pods concentrated on fewer nodes so it can remove empty ones. These goals conflict during scale-down, and the result is unnecessary pod disruption.

The timing makes this hard to fix after the fact. Pod scale-in happens first: the RS controller picks which pods to delete. Then the autoscaler reacts, notices underutilized nodes, and evicts more pods to consolidate. By that point, the spreading has already happened. Better consolidation afterward helps, but it cannot undo the suboptimal deletions.

This affects any cluster that uses both HPA and a node autoscaler. The impact scales with the frequency of scale-down events and the number of replicas. Clusters with diurnal traffic patterns, frequent deployments, or bursty workloads hit this repeatedly.

The `controller.kubernetes.io/pod-deletion-cost` annotation (KEP-2255) lets external controllers in

title: `decoratedWatcher` does not unwrap `CacheableObject` before applying decorator, breaking `defaultOnRead` for watch events
body:
### What happened?

The [`decoratedWatcher`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/decorated_watcher.go#L61) calls `d.decorator(recv.Object)` on watch events, but the object dispatched by the [watch cache](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L974) is wrapped in a `cachingObject`. Since `cachingObject` implements [`runtime.CacheableObject`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/interfaces.go#L344) but is not the underlying resource type, any decorator that relies on a type assertion silently no-ops for watch events while working correctly for GET and LIST.

For Services, the [`Store.Decorator`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/pkg/registry/core/service/storage/storage.go#L129) is set to [`defaultOnRead`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/pkg/registry/core/service/storage/storage.go#L232), which type-switches on `*api.Service` / `*api.ServiceList` to call [`defaultOnReadService`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/pkg/registry/core/service/storage/storage.go#L256). This defaults `spec.ipFamilies` (via [`defaultOnReadIPFamilies`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/pkg/registry/core/service/storage/storage.go#L280)), normalizes `spec.clusterIPs`, and drops `spec.internalTrafficPolicy` for ExternalName services. None of this runs for watch events because the `*cachingObject` wrapper falls through the type switch to the [default no-op case](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/pkg/registry/core/service/storage/storage.go#L238).

The immediate consequence observed is a KCM endpoint controller [panic](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/pkg/controller/endpoint/endpoints_controller.go#L223) (`index out of range [0] with length 0` at `svc.Spec.IPFamilies[0]`) when processing services stored in etcd without `ipFamilies` (created before dual-stack GA ~v1.23).

### What did you expect to happen?

Watch events should deliver objects with the same defaulted fields as GET/LIST responses. The `decoratedWatcher` should unwrap `CacheableObject` before calling the decorator so that type-assertion work consistently across all read paths.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a kind cluster (v1.33+)
2. Create a ClusterIP Service with a selector and matching pods
3. Strip `spec.ipFamilies` from the Service in etcd using [auger](https://github.com/etcd-io/auger) (simulates a pre-dualstack-GA service object)
4. Verify `kubectl get svc` still shows `ipFamilies: ["IPv4"]` the GET decorator masks the missing field
5. Trigger a status-only update: `kubectl patch svc <name> --subresource=status -p '{"status":{"conditions":[{"type":"Test","status":"True"}]}}'`
6. Observe: the watch event delivered to KCM has no `ipFamilies`, and the endpoint controller panics

A spec update (e.g., `kubectl annotate svc`) does NOT trigger the issue because the Service allocator runs during spec updates and backfills `ipFamilies` into etcd. Status updates bypass the allocator entirely.

### Anything else we need to know?

## Root cause:
The watch dispatch path wraps objects in `cachingObject` via [`setCachingObjects()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L913) for serialization caching (called from [`dispatchEvent()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L944)). When `decoratedWatcher.run()` calls `d.decorator(recv.Object)`, the decorator receives a `*cachingObject` instead of the underlying type (e.g., `*api.Service`). The Service decorator's [type switch](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/pkg/registry/core/service/storage/storage.go#L233) fall

title: KMSv2: Write DEK expiration is indefinitely extended despite unhealthy KMS plugin status  (StatusResponse.Healthz != "ok")
body:
### What happened?

### Tl;DR

When a KMS key is disabled/pending deletion, the apiserver's write DEK ([kmsv2PluginWriteDEKSourceMaxTTL](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5cf56a97d5ec9747371ff221e8d320e819950083/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go#L93) = 3 minutes) is never allowed to expire. Writes continue indefinitely using the cached DEK, defeating the safety mechanism designed to stop writes when the KMS is unhealthy.

### Root cause

This happens because [rotateDEKOnKeyIDChange()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5cf56a97d5ec9747371ff221e8d320e819950083/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go#L405)  extends `State.ExpirationTimestamp` before the [Healthz != "ok"](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5cf56a97d5ec9747371ff221e8d320e819950083/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go#L488-L489)  error is aggregated and returned. The function only checks if the `keyID` is structurally valid and matches the current state,  it does not check whether the plugin reported itself as healthy.




Basically, the state is stored with an extended expiration https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5cf56a97d5ec9747371ff221e8d320e819950083/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go#L406-L407  before `isKMSv2ProviderHealthyAndMaybeRotateDEK`  returns an error https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5cf56a97d5ec9747371ff221e8d320e819950083/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go#L488-L513 . Since the background health loop retries every 10 seconds [kmsv2PluginHealthzNegativeInterval](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d2c12afa4593e50a187075157d38748292b02733/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go#L92) on failure, and each retry extends the expiration by 3 minutes, the write DEK never expires.


#### Contributing factor (KMS plugin implementations)

Observed both major KMS plugin implementations return a valid `KeyId` in the StatusResponse even when reporting unhealthy status: AWS encryption provider [plugin_v2.go](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/aws-encryption-provider/blob/6e294b39447208eba7895ae33c54a0d706ac3ede/pkg/plugin/plugin_v2.go#L131-L140) and GCP Cloud KMS plugin [plugin.go](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/k8s-cloudkms-plugin/blob/fea8970a7febc9565b195a6f617d018687b73662/plugin/v2/plugin.go#L97)

Also, Apiserver should not depend on plugin implementations to omit `KeyId` during failures in order to enforce its own write safety guarantees. The `kmsv2PluginWriteDEKSourceMaxTTL` mechanism is an apiserver-level invariant , it should be enforced entirely within the apiserver by gating [rotateDEKOnKeyIDChange()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c180d6762d7ac5059d9b50457cafb0d7f4cf74a9/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go#L388-L414) on `response.Healthz == "ok"`, rather than relying on external plugin behavior to not return a structurally valid KeyId during error conditions. 



### Impact

**Security:** 

Data continues to be encrypted with a DEK whose backing CMK has been disabled/deleted. Operators expect that disabling a CMK will stop writes within minutes,  this doesn't happen.


**Operational divergence across instances creates confused experience to customer:** 

In a multi-apiserver setup, each instance generates its own independent DEK via [GenerateTransformer()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c180d6762d7ac5059d9b50457cafb0d7f4cf74a9/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/value/encrypt/envelope/kmsv2/envelope.go#L367-L418). Each instance can only decrypt objects encrypted by another instance if that other instance's DEK is present in its local read cache (an in-memory [simpleCache](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c180d6762d7ac5059d9b50457cafb0d7f4cf74a9/staging/src/k8s.io/api

title: client-go certificate manager hardcodes ECDSA P-256 key type with no way to configure it
body:
### What happened?

The `generateCSR()` function in `staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/certificate/certificate_manager.go` hardcodes the key type to ECDSA P-256:

```go
privateKey, err := ecdsa.GenerateKey(elliptic.P256(), cryptorand.Reader)
```

This means all kubelet client and server certificates generated via the certificate manager use ECDSA P-256, regardless of what key type the cluster CA uses. There is no configuration option to override this.

The kubelet client certificate on the first control plane node is initially generated by `kubeadm` using the same key type as the cluster CA (typically RSA 2048), but on subsequent rotations it switches to ECDSA P-256 because rotation goes through client-go's hardcoded path.

### What did you expect to happen?

The key type for CSR generation should be configurable via the `CertificateManager` `Config` struct, similar to how `GetUsages` is already a configurable function. For example:

```go
type Config struct {
    // ...existing fields...

    // GenerateKey allows overriding the default key generation (ECDSA P-256).
    // If nil, defaults to ecdsa.GenerateKey(elliptic.P256(), rand.Reader).
    GenerateKey func() (crypto.Signer, error)
}
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy a Kubernetes cluster with an RSA CA (default `kubeadm init` behavior).
2. Inspect the kubelet client certificate on the first control plane node — it uses RSA (same as CA).
3. Wait for certificate rotation (or force it by shortening cert lifetime).
4. After rotation, inspect the new kubelet client certificate — it is now ECDSA P-256.
5. On worker nodes, kubelet client and server certificates are ECDSA P-256 from the start.

The hardcoded line is at:
[`staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/certificate/certificate_manager.go#L767`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/certificate/certificate_manager.go#L767)

### Anything else we need to know?

- Environments requiring RSA keys (compliance, HSM compatibility, consistency with CA) cannot use built-in certificate rotation without patching client-go.
- Some deployments require ECDSA P-384 as P-256 is not considered sufficient under their security policies. The hardcoded P-256 makes this impossible without forking client-go.
- The `GetUsages` callback already handles the key-type-dependent usage selection, so the infrastructure for key-type awareness exists — only the generation itself is not configurable.

title: client-go: rest_client metrics lack resource dimensions, making client-side observability difficult
body:
### What happened?

Server-side metrics (e.g. `apiserver_request_duration_seconds`) let you measure latency per verb, resource, group, version, and scope.

However, the client-side metrics exposed by client-go's REST layer use only verb (raw HTTP method) and host as labels. This means:

  - You cannot measure client-side latency per resource. "How long do Pod LIST calls take from the controller's perspective?" is unanswerable.
  - LIST and GET are indistinguishable. The client records the raw HTTP method GET for both. The server distinguishes these as separate verbs.
  - No scope information. You cannot distinguish cluster-scoped from namespace-scoped requests.

Debugging client-side latency is difficult because the metrics lack this information.

We could add resource-aware labels to `rest_client` metrics, similar to what server-side metrics already provide:

1. We could add resource , group, version, and scope labels.
2. We could map HTTP methods to API verbs (GET vs LIST) so verb carries semantic meaning.


Additionally, the recently introduced `A Unified Identity for client-go Components for Enhanced Telemetry` ([xref](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1HUNewBqN3lk2DSHJaxKZmmhYgt0SNgp9AqpJTY6cfRM/edit?resourcekey=0-uIvQ3ezUROHa6OKjWZUzcw&tab=t.0#heading=h.qtaj715knfkg))  for client-go components provides a name label that Informers and Reflectors propagate to identify which component initiated a request. This identity could also be passed into rest_client metrics, allowing to correlate API requests back to the specific component that made them.

title: HPA controller - hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector func serializes all workers behind global exclusive mutex, causing ~ O(#Hpa*#Hpa) degradation at scale
body: ### What happened? ### TL;DR on the Issue The HPA controller's selector overlap check ([`hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L396-L422)) runs every reconciliation for every HPA and holds a [global exclusive mutex](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L398-L399) while performing O(H) work. Despite starting [multiple worker goroutines](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L217), only one can execute the overlap check at a time. At scale, **_mutex contention_** dominates wall-clock time and reconciliation cannot keep up with the resync period. ### Mutex profile **60-second sample:** ``` File: kube-controller-manager Type: delay Duration: 60.02s, Total samples = 1.35hrs (8111.81%) 1.35hrs 100% sync.(*Mutex).Unlock 0 0% ...podautoscaler.(*HorizontalController).computeReplicasForMetrics 0 0% ...podautoscaler.(*HorizontalController).hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector (99.41%) 0 0% ...podautoscaler.(*HorizontalController).validateAndParseSelector (99.92%) ``` 1.35 hours of goroutine-blocked time accumulated in 60 seconds of wall clock (8111% of wall clock duration). **Cumulative snapshot (since process start):** ``` File: kube-controller-manager Type: delay Total samples = 4.18hrs 4.18hrs 99.90% sync.(*Mutex).Unlock 0 0% ...podautoscaler.(*HorizontalController).hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector (99.25%) 0 0% ...podautoscaler.(*HorizontalController).validateAndParseSelector (99.80%) ``` 99.25% of all mutex contention in the HPA controller is in `hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector`. ### Root cause Three problems compound: #### 1. Global exclusive lock on a per-HPA operation The [`hpaSelectorsMux`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L125) is held for the [entire body](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L398-L399) of `hpasControllingPodsUnderSelector`. This includes iterating all pods, inserting each into the BiMultimap, querying associations, and cleaning up. All worker goroutines contend on this single lock regardless of namespace. #### 2. BiMultimap cache is always cold [`KeepOnly([]Key{})`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L415) destroys all temporary pod entries at the end of every call. This triggers [refCount decrement to zero](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/util/selectors/bimultimap.go#L188-L191), which deletes the `selectingByLabeled` cache entry. Every subsequent call hits the ["Cache miss. Scan selecting objects"](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/util/selectors/bimultimap.go#L138) path, iterating all HPA selectors in the BiMultimap. #### 3. A read operation implemented as write-query-delete The overlap check only needs to answer: "which existing HPA selectors match these pod labels?" That's a read query. But because the BiMultimap API currently supports "insert a labeled object, then ask who selects it," the code must [temporarily insert pods](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd297d17c816e2f86baaf7e2b21489c8346/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L403-L404) (a write), [query](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/24dbafd2

title: Metrics missing using MultiCIDRServiceAllocator
body:
### What happened?

Our initial cluster ServiceCidr was running out of available IP addresses. We created a new one which extended the existing default one. We then updated kube-apiserver's `--service-cluster-ip-range` and removed the default one, so that it will get re-created using our new extended range. Finally we removed the temporary created ServiceCidr. The end result is that we now have a single ServiceCidr in our cluster using our newly extended range. In the past, we had relied upon the metrics `kube_apiserver_clusterip_allocator_available_ips` and `kube_apiserver_clusterip_allocator_allocation_errors_total` to get notified when we are running out of IP addresses. This no longer works because these metrics are now gone.

My understanding is that we are now in the world of `MultiCIDRServiceAllocator` and KEP 1880. According to https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/[sig-redacted]/1880-multiple-service-cidrs/README.md#monitoring-requirements it should still produce these metrics (or am I reading this wrong?).

### What did you expect to happen?

The metrics `kube_apiserver_clusterip_allocator_available_ips` and `kube_apiserver_clusterip_allocator_allocation_errors_total` should still be available.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I guess you would have to do the same dance we did:

1. Create a new `ServiceCidr` which is a superset of the existing `kubernetes` one created/managed by kube-apiserver
2. Adjust the `--service-cluster-ip-range` CLI flag of kube-apiserver to match the newly created `ServiceCidr`
3. Delete the default `ServiceCidr`: `kubectl delete servicecidr kubernetes` so that kube-apiserver re-creates it with new settings
4. Delete the `ServiceCidr` from step 1

### Anything else we need to know?

Before this dance of extending the `ServiceCidr` we had those metrics. Only after extending/re-creating the default `ServiceCidr` we lost those metrics. We are still seeing metrics for other allocators:

```
$ kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep -E 'allocator_(allocated|available|allocation)'

title: client-go exec authentication plugin failures only report executable name and exit code
body:
### What happened?

When a client authentication exec plugin fails, the only error information currently returned to callers is the executable file name and the exit code. 

If the plugin runs at all, and fails, the resulting error message is always in the form:
`exec: executable /path/to/plugin failed with exit code 1`.

This limitation exists because the `clientauthentication` API lacks a `Result` or `Status` field. There is no way for exec plugins to report an error to the user. 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138769 is a proposed fix for this issue. This allows plugin implementations to report a detailed error message formatted as a `metav1.Status` object on their stdout. 

 

### What did you expect to happen?

exec plugins should be able to report useful error messages to callers on failure, just like other built-in authentication mechanisms can. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Please see tests in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138769

title: Proposal: Request HPA to preinstall backup pods for minimizing service interruption upon failures
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Introduce an optional parameter to the HPA configuration, for example `backupReplicas`, that would allow you to:

- Specify the exact number of backup pods the autoscaler should maintain alongside the nominal ones.
- Better monitor the average load against the _TARGETS_ thresholds via the _kubectl get hpa_ command.

The new structure of the HPA specification would look like:

```go
type HorizontalPodAutoscalerSpec struct {
	ScaleTargetRef CrossVersionObjectReference
	MinReplicas *int32
	MaxReplicas int32
	Metrics []MetricSpec
	Behavior *HorizontalPodAutoscalerBehavior
	BackupReplicas *int32
}
```


### Why is this needed?

When a pod fails, Kubernetes might take time before restoring another pod on a new node. Deploying a new pod involves time-consuming operations like starting pod processes, downloading container images or sometimes waiting for an available node. Preprovisioning one or several shared backup pods in addition to the nominal ones can reduce the service interruption since those time-consuming operations are already achieved before the pod failure occurs.

Suppose that a Kubernetes service is configured to load balance flows onto a replicaset bound with an HPA defined with the `minReplicas` parameter equal to (_1_ + _Backup_) and with the `maxReplicas` parameter equal to (_Nominal_ + _Backup_). For the shared protection to be efficient, the HPA should add a (_x_ + _1_)<sup>th</sup> pod in the replicaset as soon as the pods are loaded at a ratio (_x_ - _Backup_) / _x_ that depends on _x_, the number of pods already deployed.

Based solely on fixed _TARGETS_ thresholds, the current `v2` HPA version does not satisfy this requirement. By introducing the optional `backupReplicas` parameter, the HPA can decide to add or remove a pod at the right pod load ratio and in this way become fully compatible with the shared protection requirement.

title: DaemonSet status should expose why rollout pods are unavailable
body:
[[sig-redacted]]
/kind feature

The DaemonSet controller reports aggregate counts without showing whether unavailable or not-yet-updated pods are on NotReady nodes.

## What would you like to be added?

Add a DaemonSet status signal that lets rollout automation distinguish between:

- pods unavailable because the new rollout is problematic and may need rollback, and
- pods unavailable because the underlying node is NotReady, shutting down, disconnected, or under maintenance.

The second case creates problems for automation. The exact solution is up for discussion, but having a status field such as `daemonset.status.numberUnavailableOnNotReadyNodes` would be useful.

The goal is not to make the DaemonSet controller own node repair or maintenance policy. It is to expose enough information for rollout controllers, Helm hooks, operators, and humans to interpret rollout status without reimplementing their own attribution logic.

## Why is this needed?

In large clusters, DaemonSet rollout status can be ambiguous when only a few pods remain unavailable.

Example DaemonSet status from a large cluster:

```yaml
updateStrategy:
  rollingUpdate:
    maxSurge: 0
    maxUnavailable: 10%
  type: RollingUpdate
status:
  currentNumberScheduled: 100
  desiredNumberScheduled: 100
  numberAvailable: 95
  numberMisscheduled: 0
  numberReady: 95
  numberUnavailable: 5
  observedGeneration: 10
  updatedNumberScheduled: 95
```

This DaemonSet is not blocked by `maxUnavailable`; with `desiredNumberScheduled: 100` and `maxUnavailable: 10%`, the rollout budget is 10 pods. However, external rollout verification still needs to answer:

Are the remaining 5 pods unavailable because the rollout is unhealthy, or because they are on NotReady nodes?

`numberUnavailable` alone cannot answer that. It may include pods affected by rollout issues, pod readiness, `minReadySeconds`, pending/rejected pods, terminating pods, old revisions, kubelet issues, or NotReady node state.

Today, automation has to inspect Pods and often list Nodes before deciding whether the rollout should pass. That has two practical costs:

1. Every rollout verifier or operator must implement its own attribution and ignore policy.
2. In large clusters, repeated rollout checks can create additional API server and etcd load, often during periods where node lifecycle events and DaemonSet rollouts are already increasing control-plane activity.

This is especially visible for DaemonSets with broad tolerations:

```yaml
tolerations:
- operator: Exists
```

For these DaemonSets, taints do not reduce the desired node set. A NotReady node may still be counted as desired, but `numberUnavailable` does not show whether NotReady nodes are the cause of the remaining unavailability. Consumers must inspect lower-level objects to attribute the reason.

## How can we reproduce it?

One possible reproduction:

1. Create a cluster with many nodes.
2. Create a DaemonSet with `RollingUpdate`, `maxSurge: 0`, and a non-zero `maxUnavailable`.
3. Give the DaemonSet broad tolerations, such as `operator: Exists`, so node taints do not exclude most nodes from `desiredNumberScheduled`.
4. Start a DaemonSet rollout.
5. Make a small number of nodes NotReady or disconnected while leaving the Node objects present.
6. Observe that DaemonSet status reports aggregate unavailable/not-updated counts, but does not indicate whether NotReady nodes account for those counts.
7. Observe that external rollout automation must inspect Pods and often LIST Nodes to decide whether the rollout should fail or be accepted.

## Current behavior

DaemonSet status reports aggregate scheduling, availability, and update counts. It does not show how many unavailable or not-yet-updated pods are on NotReady nodes.

## Expected behavior

Kubernetes should provide a supported way to identify DaemonSet rollout unavailability caused by NotReady nodes. This could be an API status enhancement, condition, event, or documentation update.

title: Regression: modifications to suspended jobs, before JobSuspended=True is set are rejected in 1.36
body:
### What happened?

In 1.36 k8s graduated to Beta to feature gate: MutableSchedulingDirectivesForSuspendedJobs

The intention of the gate is to allow mutability of Job's scheduling directives whenever the Job is suspended. 

Previously the mutability was only allowed for Job which are "suspended" and "not started".

So, in principle the change is relaxation of conditions.

However, there is one specific scenario where the validation is stronger - for newly created Jobs for which we don't yet have the JobSuspended condition.

Here is the relevant code: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/registry/batch/job/strategy.go#L147-L155

I think we could fix the issue relatively simply be changing the mutability check into: `suspended && batchvalidation.IsConditionTrue(oldJob.Status.Conditions, batch.JobSuspended) && oldJob.Status.Active == 0` 

`suspended && (notStarted || batchvalidation.IsConditionTrue(oldJob.Status.Conditions, batch.JobSuspended)) && oldJob.Status.Active == 0`  - basically include the `notStarted` as an OR.

### What did you expect to happen?

This is discovered as it makes MultiKueue not working for K8s 1.36: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/pull/11576

This is because on the management cluster Kueue, when scheduling, attempts to inject scheduling directives to a Job which does not have the JobSuspended condition.

This can be workedaround in Kueue, but raising the point that the validation change in 1.36 is breaking.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a suspended Job managed by an external controller (as it happens when MultiKueue is used)
2. Then try to modify the Job's scheduling directives, eg inject nodeSelector while the Job is suspended (and never started)

title: TestLegacyServiceAccountTokenTracking has an impossible date-window assertion around UTC midnight
body:
`TestLegacyServiceAccountTokenTracking` in `test/integration/serviceaccount/service_account_test.go` tries to tolerate the date changing while the test runs by capturing `dateBefore` and `dateAfter`, but the assertion currently requires the observed date to equal both values:

```go
if date != dateBefore || date != dateAfter {
    t.Fatalf("Secret was labeled with wrong date: %q", date)
}
```

The same pattern is used again for the ConfigMap check later in the test.

That condition only passes when `dateBefore == dateAfter == date`. If the test spans UTC midnight, `dateBefore != dateAfter`, so no valid value can satisfy the check and the test flakes even if the implementation is correct.

I think both checks should allow either boundary date instead:

```go
if date != dateBefore && date != dateAfter {
    ...
}
```

I traced this back to the original test added in commit `569cd70a52359a294a608fb256693445a89a9dab`, and it still exists after the later flake fix in commit `6784610bebedb33f22259042c728a798c1e04b03`, which changed the concurrency/warning-count part of the test but did not update these date assertions.

If this sounds right, I can put together a small PR that only fixes the two assertions.

title: Allow BGP/anycast Services to skip kube-proxy external no-endpoints filtering
body: ### What would you like to be added? An opt-in annotation that tells kube-proxy to skip installing REJECT/DROP rules in the filter table (`KUBE-EXTERNAL-SERVICES`) for a Service's external IPs when no endpoints exist on that node. For example: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: ntp-anycast annotations: projectcalico.org/loadBalancerIPs: '["1.2.3.4"]' service.kubernetes.io/no-reject-on-no-endpoints: "true" <<< spec: type: LoadBalancer externalTrafficPolicy: Local ports: - name: ntp protocol: UDP port: 123 targetPort: 1123 selector: app: chrony status: loadBalancer: ingress: - ip: 1.2.3.4 # anycast VIP advertised via BGP ipMode: VIP ``` When `no-reject-on-no-endpoints: "true"` is set and no local endpoints exist, kube-proxy would not install the filter rule. Traffic would fall through to normal kernel routing, where the BGP speaker (or similar) handles failover. This allows BGP/anycast deployments to rely on routing failover to a nearby cluster/region. ### Why is this needed? kube-proxy installs filter rules in `KUBE-EXTERNAL-SERVICES` to REJECT or DROP traffic to external IPs when no endpoints are available. This is correct for standard Services — it gives clients an immediate ICMP error instead of a timeout. However, in BGP/anycast deployments this behavior prevents routing failover. The BGP speaker withdraws the route when endpoints disappear, so the kernel routing table would naturally send the packet off-node. But kube-proxy's filter rule intercepts and drops the packet before routing takes effect. Example topology: When local service is working: ```shell › kubectl get endpointslices ntp-anycast-t7n2l NAME ADDRESSTYPE PORTS ENDPOINTS ntp-anycast-t7n2l IPv4 123 100.90.14.133 ``` Output from the node in `Cluster A` with respective pod running: ```shell # iptables-save | grep 1.2.3.4 -A KUBE-SERVICES -d 1.2.3.4/32 -p udp -m comment --comment "test/ntp-anycast:ntp-udp-123 loadbalancer IP" -m udp --dport 123 -j KUBE-EXT-IL6URECE27T65EPH ``` Other node in same cluster `Cluster A` (e.g. with pods consuming this service): ```shell # iptables-save | grep 1.2.3.4 -A KUBE-SERVICES -d 1.2.3.4/32 -p udp -m comment --comment "test/ntp-anycast:ntp-udp-123 loadbalancer IP" -m udp --dport 123 -j KUBE-EXT-IL6URECE27T65EPH -A KUBE-EXTERNAL-SERVICES -d 1.2.3.4/32 -p udp -m comment --comment "test/ntp-anycast:ntp-udp-123 has no local endpoints" -m udp --dport 123 -j DROP ``` When local service fails, we expect a fallback to another region. ```shell › kubectl get endpointslices ntp-anycast-t7n2l NAME ADDRESSTYPE PORTS ENDPOINTS ntp-anycast-t7n2l IPv4 123 ``` Output any node in `Cluster A`: ```shell # iptables-save | grep 1.2.3.4 -A KUBE-EXTERNAL-SERVICES -d 1.2.3.4/32 -p udp -m comment --comment "test/ntp-anycast:ntp-udp-123 has no endpoints" -m udp --dport 123 -j REJECT --reject-with icmp-port-unreachable ``` Due to above rule: - Nodes in `Cluster A` are able to communicate with `1.2.3.4/32` service in `Cluster 2` - Pods in `Cluster A` are *not* able to communicate with `1.2.3.4/32` service in `Cluster 2` and get `connection refused` error message This proposed approach would follow the existing annotation-based extension pattern used by Service features such as `service.kubernetes.io/topology-mode` and load balancer source ranges. Use cases: anycast UDP services, anycast ingress, and active-active multi-cluster Services with shared VIPs. [[sig-redacted]] /kind feature /area kube-proxy

title: Investigate nftables startup performance at scale
body:
@npinaeva had done some nftables scaling testing a while back and determined that nftables kube-proxy startup time was much slower than iptables kube-proxy startup time. 

#130119 fixed this for the _restart_ case (kube-proxy starting up when there's already a mostly-correct ruleset present and we just need to synchronize to make sure we get any changes that happened while kube-proxy wasn't running), but it didn't address the "cold start" case. In particular, when adding a new node to a large cluster, kube-proxy on that node will have to sync the entire ruleset starting from nothing.

It's possible that #135800 and #136499 may have fixed this... we hadn't gotten as far as debugging _exactly_ what made things slow.

So part 1 is: see if starting up a fresh kube-proxy in a large cluster (lots of services and endpoints) is still slow (either in general, or specifically compared to the iptables backend).

If it turns out we do still need improvements, part 2 is to do that. One thing to try is splitting the transaction up into multiple steps rather than adding every single new service and endpoint all at once. In particular, if we are starting from a state where the `kube-proxy` table does not yet exist, then:

- The endpoint chains and affinity sets can be created first, potentially split up into multiple transactions if there are a lot of them.
- The service chains can be created next, potentially split up into multiple transactions if there are a lot of them.
- Once all the service chains exist, we can fill in all the service sets and maps. Again, at least in theory, this could be split up into multiple transactions, though I'm not sure if that would have better or worse performance.

title: WAS: Align Job Controller Integration with WAS Controller Integration APIs
body:
As WAS evolves, controller integrations should not each define their own bespoke API patterns, helper logic, or behavioral contracts. [KEP 6089](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/6089) defines the broader direction for providing standard API building blocks, shared libraries, and guidelines that enable workload controllers to design native APIs for consuming WAS features.

The Job controller integration should be updated to follow that direction and serve as an implementation aligned with the shared controller-integration model.

title: PV controller emits spurious Warning ClaimMisbound event for volume populator prime PVCs
body:
### What happened?

Volume populators (e.g. [hello-populator](https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/lib-volume-populator/tree/master/example/hello-populator)) create a temporary "prime" PVC, provision and populate a PV through it, then rebind the PV to the original PVC. After the rebind, the prime PVC always receives a `Warning ClaimMisbound "Two claims are bound to the same volume, this one is bound incorrectly"` event. This is a false positive — the rebind is the designed and expected flow, not an error condition.

The `Lost` phase transition on the prime PVC is correct and necessary (lib-volume-populator polls for it as confirmation that the rebind succeeded), but the warning event creates noise for users and monitoring systems on every populator operation.

### What did you expect to happen?

The PV controller should recognize that a deliberate populator rebind is not an error condition. The prime PVC should still transition to `Lost`, but the event should be downgraded to `Normal` with an appropriate message (e.g. `Normal ClaimLost "Claim is being replaced by a volume populator and is no longer needed"`).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy the [hello-populator](https://github.com/kubernetes-csi/lib-volume-populator/tree/master/example/hello-populator) example volume populator
2. Create a `Hello` CR and a PVC with a `dataSourceRef` pointing to it
3. Wait for population to complete and the PV to be rebound to the original PVC
4. Observe the `Warning ClaimMisbound` event on the prime PVC

This happens on every populator operation, 100% of the time.

### Anything else we need to know?

This affects any volume populator built on lib-volume-populator (hello-populator, CDI, etc.). It was observed in practice as a contributing factor in kubevirt/kubevirt#17724, where `ClaimMisbound` events during volume migration added confusion when debugging and triggered false alerts.

`spec.volumeName` is immutable once set, so the populator cannot clear it on the prime PVC before rebinding — the only fix is on the PV controller side.

## Background

The following feature gates are currently deprecated and default to false:

They were introduced as compatibility switches for the old kubelet CSR behavior around v1.31:

- AllowDNSOnlyNodeCSR allows kubelet serving CSRs without Node IPs, using DNS names only.
- AllowInsecureKubeletCertificateSigningRequests disables stricter NodeRestriction validation for kubelet CSR signers.

Both gates are still present in the codebase and documentation, although the v1.31 change notes described them as temporary compatibility gates.

## Proposal

I would like to clean up these deprecated feature gates in phases:

1. Confirm whether these gates can be locked to their default value `false`.
2. Add `LockToDefault: true` if required by the feature gate lifecycle.
3. After the required compatibility window, remove:

title: Job controller manageJob() returns active=0 during backoff, causing "cannot set more ready pods than active" status update rejection
body:
### What happened?

When the Job controller's `manageJob()` function determines that replacement pods are needed but a backoff timer is active (due to recent pod failures), it returns `active=0` to the caller. The caller uses this value to set `job.Status.Active=0` in a status update, while `job.Status.Ready` retains the real informer-computed count. The apiserver validation `RejectMoreReadyThanActivePods` (GA in 1.33 via `JobManagedBy`) correctly rejects this inconsistent update with 422.

Because the status update fails, the controller cannot:
- Flush `uncountedTerminatedPods`
- Remove `batch.kubernetes.io/job-tracking` finalizers from terminated pods

This causes pods to appear stuck in Terminating state and job status to become stale.

**Root cause:** Two locations in `manageJob()` return a hardcoded `0` instead of the real `active` count when backoff is active:

```go
// Location 1: global backoff
if remainingTime > 0 {
    jm.enqueueSyncJobWithDelay(logger, job, remainingTime)
    return 0, metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated, nil  // BUG: should be `active`
}

// Location 2: per-index backoff
if remainingTime > 0 {
    jm.enqueueSyncJobWithDelay(logger, job, remainingTime)
    return 0, metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated, nil  // BUG: should be `active`
}
```

The caller sets `job.Status.Active = active` (the returned 0), while `job.Status.Ready` stays at the informer count (e.g., 5). Result: `5 > 0` → 422.

The `0` was likely a "don't care" value from before `RejectMoreReadyThanActivePods` validation existed. Every other return path in `manageJob` returns the real active count.

### What did you expect to happen?

The backoff early-return in `manageJob()` should return the real active pod count (unchanged, since no pods were created or deleted), not 0.

Proposed fix:
```diff
     if remainingTime > 0 {
         jm.enqueueSyncJobWithDelay(logger, job, remainingTime)
-        return 0, metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated, nil
+        return active, metrics.JobSyncActionPodsCreated, nil
     }
```

Returning `active` (initialized at top of `manageJob` as `int32(len(jobCtx.activePods))`) means "I didn't create or delete any pods" — the correct semantics for a backoff deferral.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```bash
# 1. Create a Job
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: repro-ready-active
  namespace: default
spec:
  parallelism: 30
  completions: 30
  backoffLimit: 500
  completionMode: Indexed
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: worker
        image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "10m"
            memory: "16Mi"
EOF

# 2. Wait for all pods to be Running+Ready
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l job-name=repro-ready-active --timeout=120s

# 3. Force-delete 25 pods simultaneously
kubectl get pods -l job-name=repro-ready-active -o name | head -25 | \
  xargs -P25 kubectl delete --force --grace-period=0

# 4. Observe: job status is frozen, KCM logs show error
kubectl get job repro-ready-active -o jsonpath='active={.status.active} ready={.status.ready} failed={.status.failed}'
# Output: active=30 ready=30 failed=   (stale — doesn't reflect reality)

# KCM logs show:
# "Unhandled Error" err="syncing job: tracking status: adding uncounted pods to status:
#   Job.batch \"repro-ready-active\" is invalid: status.ready: Invalid value: 5:
#   cannot set more ready pods than active"

# 5. Bug self-resolves after ~10 min when backoff expires (if no new failures arrive)
```

### Anything else we need to know?

- The bug fires on any multi-pod Job that experiences a pod failure while other pods are still Ready. For single failures (10s backoff), it produces a few 422 errors that self-resolve. For mass failures (spot reclamation, node failure → backoff capped at 10 min), it causes visible stuck pods and stale status for the full backoff duration.
- No data l

title: [Feature Request] Native Zone/Topology-Aware Scaling in HPA to complement Topology Aware Routing
body:
### What would you like to be added?

### Description
When combining **Topology Aware Routing** (`service.kubernetes.io/topology-mode: Auto`) with the **HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA)**, there is a systemic architectural gap that risks localized pod starvation during scale-out events, and extreme endpoint imbalance during scale-in events. 

Currently, the HPA evaluates resource utilization (e.g., CPU, Memory) as a global, deployment-wide aggregate average. However, Topology Aware Routing deliberately isolates traffic to localized Availability Zones (AZs). 

This decoupled behavior creates a "Thundering Herd" trap during spikes, and a "Starvation" trap during downscaling, because the network routing layer is highly topology-aware while the autoscaling control loop is completely topology-blind.


### Why is this needed?


### Use Case
We run high-throughput microservices on AWS (EKS) distributed across 3 Availability Zones. To mitigate high cross-AZ data transfer costs ("Cross-AZ Tax") and lower network latency, we rely heavily on Topology Aware Routing. 

We face two distinct structural failures due to the lack of zone-aware autoscaling:

1. **The Scale-Out Trap (Localized Overload):** During localized network shifts or zone-specific traffic spikes, pods in a single AZ (e.g., `us-east-1a`) take 100% of that localized load. If `us-east-1a` pods hit 95% CPU utilization while pods in `us-east-1b` and `us-east-1c` remain idle at 10%, the cluster-wide average sits at ~38%. The HPA fails to trigger, and the pods in the stressed zone crash due to localized resource starvation.
2. **The Scale-In Trap (Zone Depletion):** When traffic drops globally and the HPA triggers a downscale event, the underlying ReplicaSet controller selects pods for termination without respecting zone distribution. It frequently terminates a disproportionate number of pods from a single zone. This leaves that specific zone entirely depleted of endpoints, breaking the path for subsequent localized traffic and forcing expensive, high-latency cross-AZ failovers.

### Proposed Solution / Architectural Approaches
We request native support for zone/topology-awareness within the core autoscaling and lifecycle framework:

1. **Topology-Aware Scale-Out Policy:** Introduce a configuration field in the HPA spec (e.g., `scalingPolicy.topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone`) that evaluates metrics per topology domain. If *any single zone* breaches the target utilization threshold, the HPA should proactively trigger a scale-up event.
2. **Topology-Aware Scale-In (Downscaling):** Ensure that when the HPA reduces the replica count, the scale-in mechanism balances pod terminations proportionally across all active topology domains. The controller must prevent downscaling from leaving a specific zone starved of healthy endpoints.
3. **Handling Soft Constraints (`ScheduleAnyway`):** If a deployment utilizes `whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway`, a Zone-Aware HPA should exploit this flexibility. During a localized spike, it should scale up replicas specifically within the hurting topology domain, allowing a temporary skew to absorb the traffic. During the subsequent scale-in event, the controller must prioritize deleting pods from the skewed zone to automatically return the cluster to its baseline balanced topology spread.

### Related Existing Issue
* **kubernetes/kubernetes #124149** 


### Additional Context
Current ecosystem workarounds require engineers to deploy entirely independent, duplicated Deployments and HPAs per AZ (e.g., `frontend-az-a`, `frontend-az-b`). This completely breaks standard GitOps principles, bloat CI/CD pipelines, and forces rigid, static replica constraints. Native lifecycle zone-awareness is required to bridge the gap between how Kubernetes routes traffic and how it manages compute capacity.

title: kube-proxy IPVS with mh scheduler may route traffic to unavailable destinations without mh-fallback
body:
### What happened?

When kube-proxy is configured to use IPVS with the `mh` (Maglev Hashing) scheduler, traffic may fail during endpoint transitions when some backend destinations become unavailable.

The issue happens because IPVS `mh` preserves `last_weight` internally even after a destination weight is updated to `0`. As a result, the Maglev lookup table may still contain references to destinations that are no longer eligible to receive traffic.

Without the `mh-fallback` flag enabled, IPVS may fail to select another healthy destination and instead return:

```text
no destination available
```

This can lead to transient traffic failures during pod termination, rolling updates, endpoint churn, or similar scenarios where backend availability changes dynamically.

A proposed fix was implemented in the following PR:

* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138688

The PR enables `FlagFallBack` together with `FlagSourceHash` for the `mh` scheduler in kube-proxy IPVS mode.


### What did you expect to happen?

When a destination becomes unavailable (for example, weight becomes `0` during pod termination), IPVS using the `mh` scheduler should fall back to another healthy backend destination instead of returning `no destination available`.

Traffic disruption should be minimized during endpoint transitions and rolling updates.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Kubernetes cluster with kube-proxy running in IPVS mode.

2. Configure kube-proxy to use the `mh` scheduler.

3. Deploy a Service with multiple backend Pods.

4. Generate traffic that consistently hashes to a specific backend.

5. Terminate or make one of the backend Pods unavailable so that its weight becomes `0`.

6. Observe that some requests may fail with behavior corresponding to:

```text
no destination available
```

7. Observe IPVS state during the transition:

```bash
ipvsadm -Ln --stats
ipvsadm -Ln --persistent
```

The issue is related to the Maglev lookup table still referencing destinations whose effective weight is no longer usable.

A proposed fix is available here:

* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138688


### Anything else we need to know?

This issue appears to be specific to the interaction between Kubernetes kube-proxy IPVS mode and Linux IPVS `mh` scheduler behavior.

The Linux kernel implementation preserves `last_weight`, which may cause stale destination references to remain in the Maglev lookup table during transitions.

Enabling the IPVS `mh-fallback` behavior allows IPVS to select another healthy backend when the originally selected destination is unavailable.

Related PR:

* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138688

kube-proxy nftables: sync time grows super-linearly with Service count
body: ### What happened? Our production clusters run kube-proxy in `ipvs` mode. We evaluated migrating to `nftables` mode and observed that `kube-proxy` takes a long time to complete a sync, with the `nft` process at 100% CPU for most of that time. This looks related to [#135639](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135639), which was addressed in v1.36. We are testing on v1.36.1 and still see multi-minute syncs. The two dominant costs we measure are: 1. the `ListAll` (`nft --json --terse list table ip kube-proxy`) that runs on every sync, including incremental syncs, and 1. the full sync re-emitting the entire table even when almost nothing changed. #### How we measured We created different numbers of Services/EndpointSlices in a test cluster and read kube-proxy logs at `--v=2`. A sync logs three lines: ``` I0529 17:51:15.687847 1 proxier.go:1094] "Syncing nftables rules" ipFamily="IPv4" fullSync=true I0529 17:52:18.984398 1 proxier.go:1712] "Reloading service nftables data" ipFamily="IPv4" numServices=44125 numEndpoints=44152 I0529 18:07:59.283867 1 proxier.go:1088] "SyncProxyRules complete" ipFamily="IPv4" elapsed="16m43.895505566s" ``` - ListAll time is roughly the gap between `"Syncing nftables rules"` and `"Reloading service nftables data"`. During this window `nft --json --terse list table ip kube-proxy` runs at 100% CPU. (This window also includes a small stale-chain delete transaction, which is negligible at these scales.) - Total time is the `elapsed=` value on `"SyncProxyRules complete"`. #### Test environment - Instance: `m6a.4xlarge` - kube-proxy: v1.36.1, `mode: nftables`. Default sync params: `minSyncPeriod=1s syncPeriod=30s maxSyncPeriod=1h0m0s`. - calico-node: v3.31.3 - Kernel: Linux 7.0 (Ubuntu 26.04); also reproduced on Linux 7.1-rc4 - Control plane: v1.33.7 - kubelet: v1.33.7 > We ran kube-proxy v1.36.1, despite the version skew against the v1.33.7 control plane and kubelet, to include the v1.36 nftables improvements (#135800, #136499). We believe the behavior we measured does not depend on the control plane or kubelet version: it is node-local nftables programming, driven only by the number of Services/EndpointSlices. If that assumption is wrong, please let us know and we can re-test on a version-matched cluster. Our production clusters reach ~44k Services at an almost 1:1 Service-to-endpoint ratio. That is a much larger Service count than #135639's repro (~1k–5k Services, with high endpoints-per-Service). So the cost here is driven by the number of Services/chains, not just endpoint fan-out, and it appears at Service counts well beyond what #135639 tested. No production workloads run on the test cluster. To trigger incremental syncs, a script creates and deletes 50 Services every 30 seconds. #### Results `fullSync=true` (full sync) vs `fullSync=false` (incremental). Each cell is the p50 across the collected syncs at that scale; the ListAll and Total values are taken from the same sync (the one at p50 of Total). | N (services ~ endpoints) | incremental — ListAll | incremental — Total | full — ListAll | full — Total | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 4,125 | 874 ms | 878 ms | 939 ms | 5.11 s | | 14,125 | 7.25 s | 7.49 s | 7.45 s | 58.25 s | | 24,125 | 20.44 s | 20.76 s | 21.48 s | 3m11.10s | | 34,125 | 39.61 s | 40.30 s | 47.19 s | 8m13.51s | | 44,125 | 1m9.01s | 1m10.14s | 1m3.30s | 16m43.90s | | 44,125 (empty kube-proxy table) | — | — | 284 ms | 4m46.84s | Observations: - From 4k to 44k Services (~11× the count), incremental sync grew ~80× and full sync grew ~197×. The growth is much steeper than linear in the number of Services. - Incremental sync is almost entirely `ListAll`. The actual write is small (<2s even at 44k); the rest is reading the whole table to discover existing chains/affinity sets for cleanup. - Full sync = `ListAll` + re-emitting

title: kube-proxy nftables: entire sync fails when any single Service generates a comment exceeding 128 characters
body:
__What happened?__

When running kube-proxy in `mode: nftables`, if any Service causes kube-proxy to generate an nftables comment exceeding the Linux kernel's 128-character limit, __the entire nftables transaction is rejected and no service routing rules are applied on that sync cycle__. kube-proxy retries every 30 seconds and fails every time until the offending Service is removed. During this time, __all ClusterIP routing is broken cluster-wide__, including kube-dns.

__How to reproduce__

1. Run a cluster with kube-proxy in `mode: nftables` (recommended default since Kubernetes 1.35)
2. Create a Service where the combined kube-proxy comment string `<namespace>/<service-name>:<port-name>` exceeds 128 characters

A realistic example:

- Namespace: `loft-acme-platform-services-team-dev-v-shared-workloads-ns-001` __(62 chars ✅ valid k8s namespace)__
- Service name: `my-api-svc-x-my-api-namespace-x-acme-shared-vcluster--a1b2c3d4e` __(63 chars ✅ valid k8s service name)__
- kube-proxy comment: `loft-acme-platform-services-team-dev-v-shared-workloads-ns-001/my-api-svc-x-my-api-namespace-x-acme-shared-vcluster--a1b2c3d4e:http` → __131 characters ❌ kernel rejects__

Both the namespace (62 chars) and the service name (63 chars) are individually valid Kubernetes DNS labels (≤63 chars each) and are accepted by the Kubernetes API. It is only the __combined string that kube-proxy constructs for the nftables comment__ — `<namespace>/<name>:<port>` — that exceeds the 128-char kernel limit.

This scenario occurs naturally with tools like __vCluster__, which syncs virtual-cluster Services to the host namespace using the pattern `<svc>-x-<ns>-x-<vcluster>--<hash>`. vCluster correctly truncates the service name to ≤63 chars per Kubernetes spec. However, when combined with a long management namespace name (e.g. `loft-<team>-<env>-v-<vcluster>`), the resulting nftables comment string can exceed 128 characters.

__What you expected to happen__

kube-proxy should either:

- Truncate the nftables comment to ≤128 characters (or omit it entirely) and continue syncing all other service rules successfully, OR
- Skip only the offending Service and continue applying rules for all others

__What actually happened__

kube-proxy logs show the following error on every sync attempt (every 30 seconds):

```javascript
E proxier.go:1788] "nftables sync failed" err=<
    /dev/stdin:1473:84-216: Error: comment too long, 128 characters maximum allowed
    add element ip kube-proxy no-endpoint-services { 10.96.1.100 . tcp . 80 comment "loft-acme-platform-services-team-dev-v-shared-workloads-ns-001/my-api-svc-x-my-api-namespace-x-acme-shared-vcluster--a1b2c3d4e:http" : goto reject-chain }
                                                                                     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
 > ipFamily="IPv4"
I proxier.go:1143] "Sync failed" ipFamily="IPv4" retryingTime="30s"
```

The sync fails __atomically__ — nftables applies rules in a single transaction, so one bad comment causes the __entire ruleset to be rejected__. This means zero ClusterIP routing rules exist on any node during the failure window.

__Impact__

- All Kubernetes Services become unreachable via ClusterIP on all nodes simultaneously
- `kube-dns` ClusterIP is unreachable → DNS stops working for all pods cluster-wide
- Workloads that depend on DNS (e.g. StatefulSets using headless service DNS for peer discovery such as etcd HA clusters) cannot initialize
- The failure is silent from a pod perspective — packets are dropped, not refused with an error
- Only removing the offending Service restores normal operation

__Kubernetes version__

```javascript
Server Version: v1.35.0
```

__kube-proxy mode__

```yaml
mode: nftables
```

__OS / kernel__

Talos Linux, kernel 6.x (nftables native mode)

__Suggested fix__

The nftables comment is purely for human readability — it has no functi

title: Windows KubeProxy fails to recreate LoadBalancer after HNS restart with error "hcnCreateLoadBalancer failed in Win32: Cannot create a file when that file already exists. (0xb7)"
body:
### What happened?

During HNS restart stress scenarios combined with rapid pod scale operations, Windows KubeProxy intermittently fails to recreate LoadBalancers and logs the following error:

``` hcnCreateLoadBalancer failed in Win32: Cannot create a file when that file already exists. (0xb7) ```

While HNS was temporarily unavailable, KubeProxy attempted to reconcile proxy rules. During this window:

- GetHNSNetwork failed because HNS was down.
- KubeProxy proceeded with LoadBalancer cleanup logic.
- GetLoadBalancer calls also failed due to HNS unavailability.
- KubeProxy incorrectly interpreted these failures as the LoadBalancer being absent and reset the internal LoadBalancer ID/state.

However, the actual HNS LoadBalancer objects were never deleted. After HNS restarted, the LoadBalancers were restored through the HNS backup/restore (rehydration) mechanism.
Later, when KubeProxy attempted to recreate the same LoadBalancer/frontend configuration, the operation failed because the LoadBalancer already existed in HNS.

### What did you expect to happen?

KubeProxy should treat HNS unavailability as a transient failure and avoid resetting/deleting LoadBalancer state when HNS APIs are temporarily inaccessible.
KubeProxy should:

- Distinguish transient HNS communication failures from actual “LoadBalancer not found” conditions.
- Retry reconciliation after HNS becomes healthy instead of assuming LoadBalancer absence.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Kubernetes Service backed by a deployment with 8 pods.
2. Continuously restart HNS in a loop with a 100 ms sleep interval (100 iterations).
3. Simultaneously scale the deployment up and down in a loop with a 100 ms sleep interval (100 iterations).
4. Observe repeated LoadBalancer creation failures in KubeProxy logs.

Example log monitoring command:

``` cat C:\k\kubeproxy.err.log | sls "hcnCreateLoadBalancer failed in Win32" ```

Observed error:

``` hcnCreateLoadBalancer failed in Win32: Cannot create a file when that file already exists. (0xb7) ```

### Anything else we need to know?

The issue appears to be caused by a race between:

- HNS availability during restart/recovery, and
- KubeProxy reconciliation logic.

The problem is specifically observed when:

- SyncProxyRules executes while HNS is temporarily unavailable.
- KubeProxy resets LoadBalancer state based on transient HNS API failures.
- HNS later restores existing LoadBalancers through rehydration.

This leaves KubeProxy and HNS state inconsistent, causing duplicate LoadBalancer creation attempts.

### What happened?

title: kubectl apply --dry-run=client  may fail for CRD resource with a cryptic error message
body:
### What happened?

`kubectl apply --dry-run=client` fails for existing CRD resources with an error
"applying patch locally: expected a struct, but received a nil". 


### What did you expect to happen?

The command should perform successful dry-run.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run the following script, which creates a CRD and the tries to perform
an apply with the `--dry-run=client` option:

```
#!/bin/sh
set -x -e

cat > "crd.yaml" << 'EOF'
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: bugs.bug-repro.example.com
spec:
  group: bug-repro.example.com
  names:
    kind: Bug
    plural: bugs
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
EOF

cat > "crd-modified.yaml" << 'EOF'
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: bugs.bug-repro.example.com
  labels:
    bug-repro: "true"
spec:
  group: bug-repro.example.com
  names:
    kind: Bug
    plural: bugs
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
EOF

kubectl apply -f crd.yaml

kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f crd-modified.yaml
```

The output:
```
+ cat
+ cat
+ kubectl apply -f crd.yaml
customresourcedefinition.apiextensions.k8s.io/bugs.bug-repro.example.com created
+ kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f crd-modified.yaml
error: error when applying patch:

to:
Resource: "apiextensions.k8s.io/v1, Resource=customresourcedefinitions", GroupVersionKind: "apiextensions.k8s.io/v1, Kind=CustomResourceDefinition"
Name: "bugs.bug-repro.example.com", Namespace: ""
for: "crd-modified.yaml": applying patch locally: expected a struct, but received a nil
```


### Anything else we need to know?

**Other versions affected**

Reproduces also with kubectl 1.36.0

**An attempt at root cause analysis**

The problem is in 'k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/apply/patcher.go':

1. PatchLocal is called for --dry-run=client. It calls patchSimple with the localApply=true. (the last argument):

``` 
func (p *Patcher) PatchLocal(current runtime.Object, modified []byte, errOut io.Writer) ([]byte, runtime.Object, error) {
	return p.patchSimple(current, modified, "", "", errOut, true)
}
```

Below is patchSimple(). 

At lines 111 and 136 it determines whether the resource supports StrategicMergePatch using OpenAPI and OpenAPI V3 schemas and tries to produce such a patch. 

CustomResourceDefinition is one of such resource kinds, so it will create a patch and set  `patchType` to StrategicMergePatchType. 

patch!=nil, so it will not enter the block on line 149.

The applied resource differs from the current version ,so patch won't be empty,
so it will continue after the check on line 168.

localApply=true, so it will enter the block at line 171

Here on 174 it will call `scheme.Scheme.New(p.Mapping.GroupVersionKind)`, which will fail because CRD is in 'apiextensions.k8s.io/v1', apiextensions are not  builtin k8s types, so the call will fail. 

The code skips checking error status (probably it assumes (erroneously) that StrategicMerge patch always comes from line 149).

So after ignoring the error it calls `strategicpatch.StrategicMergePatch(current, patch, versionedObj)` with versionedObj==nil.

This call fails with the cryptic error "expected a struct, but received a nil" 


```
 98	func (p *Patcher) patchSimple(obj runtime.Object, modified []byte, namespace, name string, errOut io.Writer, localApply bool) ([]byte, runtime.Object, error) {
    99		// Serialize the current configuration of the object from the server.
   100		current, err := runtime.Encode(unstructured.UnstructuredJSONScheme, obj)
   101		if err != nil {
   102			return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("serializing current configuration from:\n%v\nfor: %w", obj, err)
   103		}
       
   104		// Retrieve the original configuration of the object from the annotation.
   1

title: PDB maxUnavailable cannot compute expectedPods when a pod's direct controller owner does not implement /scale but a scalable ancestor exists
body:
## What happened

The disruption controller computes `expectedPods` for a PDB using `maxUnavailable` by calling the `/scale` subresource on each matched pod's **direct** controller owner (`metav1.GetControllerOf(pod)` → scale lookup in `pkg/controller/disruption/disruption.go`, `getExpectedScale` / `getPodControllerFromScale`).

When the direct owner does not implement `/scale`, the lookup errors and the PDB falls back to `expectedPods: 0` → `disruptionsAllowed: 0`, emitting:

```
Warning  CalculateExpectedPodCountFailed
  Failed to calculate the number of expected pods:
  <resource> does not implement the scale subresource
```

This blocks **all** voluntary evictions for the protected pods, even when a *scalable* resource exists higher in the ownership chain.

## Why this matters beyond one project

This is a general limitation for any operator/CRD pattern with multi-level ownership, where the immediately-owning object is a per-instance (non-scalable) resource but a higher-level controller is scalable. A concrete, widely-deployed example is KubeVirt:

```
virt-launcher Pod  →  VirtualMachineInstance   (direct owner, NOT scalable)
                   →  VirtualMachine
                   →  VirtualMachinePool        (scalable — implements /scale)
```

`VirtualMachinePool` implements `/scale`, but the disruption controller never reaches it because it stops at the direct owner (`VirtualMachineInstance`). Result: `maxUnavailable` PDBs are unusable for these workloads and users must fall back to `minAvailable`. (See kubevirt/kubevirt#18063 for the downstream report.)

## Current behavior

`getExpectedScale` resolves only the direct `controllerRef` and attempts a single scale lookup against it. There is no traversal of the `ownerReferences` chain.

## Proposed enhancement

When the direct controller owner does not implement `/scale`, walk the `controllerRef` chain upward (`owner → owner-of-owner → …`) and use the **nearest ancestor that implements `/scale`** to compute `expectedPods`. Stop at the first scalable ancestor, or fall back to the current behavior if none exists.

Semantically this is correct: when many pods resolve to the same scalable ancestor (deduplicated by controller UID, as the controller already does), `expectedPods` becomes that ancestor's `scale.spec.replicas` — i.e. the real desired count of the workload the PDB is protecting.

### Open design questions (likely KEP material)

1. **Object lookups for intermediate owners.** Traversal requires GET-ing each intermediate owner object to read its `ownerReferences`. The disruption controller today only has typed finders for built-in workload types plus the polymorphic scale client. Walking arbitrary CRD chains needs a dynamic/metadata client and correspondingly broad RBAC. What is the right scoping (e.g. bounded depth, only follow `controller: true` refs)?
2. **Depth bound & cycle protection.** Cap traversal depth and guard against cyclic/malformed `ownerReferences`.
3. **Ambiguity.** If multiple matched pods resolve to *different* scalable ancestors, sum per-ancestor scales (the existing dedup-by-UID logic already handles this once ancestors are correctly identified).
4. **Backward compatibility.** Behavior only changes for pods whose direct owner is non-scalable today (currently a hard failure), so this is strictly an improvement — no regression for existing scalable-direct-owner cases.

## Alternatives considered

- **Implement `/scale` on the direct owner** (e.g. add it to the per-instance resource). Rejected as a general solution: it forces a `spec.replicas` field onto inherently-singleton resources and advertises horizontal scalability that does not exist, confusing HPA/`kubectl scale`/GitOps tooling.
- **Use `minAvailable`.** Works today and needs no change, but does not give users the `maxUnavailable` semantics they ask for. Acceptable workaround, not a fix.

## Environment

- Kubernetes: behavior confirmed from `pkg/controller/disruption/disruption.go` (`getExp

title: kube-proxy: stale UDP conntrack entries are never cleaned up when a service scales down to zero endpoints
body:
### What happened?

When a UDP service with active senders is scaled down to zero endpoints, the conntrack entries established while the endpoints existed are never removed. The conntrack reconciler introduced in v1.32 (#127318) skips services without serving endpoints:

```go
// pkg/proxy/conntrack/cleanup.go
// a Service without endpoints does not require to clean the conntrack entries associated.
if endpoints.Len() == 0 {
    continue
}
```

The `REJECT` rule installed for a service with no endpoints does not help for those pre-existing flows: packets are DNATed to the (deleted) endpoint IP by conntrack before the filter rule, which matches on the service ClusterIP, can be evaluated. For one-way UDP traffic (statsd/dogstatsd-style, conntrack entries permanently `[UNREPLIED]`), every packet refreshes the 30s `nf_conntrack_udp_timeout`, so the stale entries and the blackholed traffic persist indefinitely.

In our production case (statsd at ~64k pkt/s cluster-wide), all senders kept DNAT-ing to the deleted pod IP for 13 hours. All that traffic converges on the node that owns the deleted pod IP's CIDR block and is dropped there in `NET_RX`, which held a single 8-core node at ~60-73% softirq for the whole duration. Recovery is instant once the service gets an endpoint again, because the reconciler then processes the service and deletes every entry whose reply-source is not the new endpoint.

Observed evidence on v1.33.5 (iptables mode, controlled reproduction, ~3.5 min after scaling to 0, kube-proxy already synced):

```
# REJECT rule is installed:
-A KUBE-SERVICES -d 10.0.200.123/32 -p udp -m comment --comment "test/udp-sink:statsd has no endpoints" -j REJECT --reject-with icmp-port-unreachable

# yet the stale entry persists and keeps refreshing (pod 10.244.5.127 deleted minutes ago):
udp 17 29 src=10.244.9.181 dst=10.0.200.123 sport=12345 dport=9125 [UNREPLIED] src=10.244.5.127 dst=10.244.9.181 sport=9125 dport=12345

# reconciler ran but deleted nothing:
kubeproxy_conntrack_reconciler_deleted_entries_total{ip_family="IPv4"} 1151   # unchanged

# after scaling back to 1 replica: counter 1151 -> 1152, entry deleted, traffic restored instantly
```

This is a regression versus <=1.31: the event-based cleanup (`DeletedUDPEndpoints` in the pre-reconciler `CleanStaleEntries`) cleared entries for every deleted UDP endpoint regardless of how many endpoints remained, so the N->0 transition was covered.

### What did you expect to happen?

Scaling a UDP service to zero endpoints removes the conntrack entries DNAT-ing to the deleted endpoints, the same way scaling from N to M>0 does. New packets then hit the `REJECT` rule (which also prevents new conntrack entries from being confirmed), and senders receive ICMP port-unreachable instead of blackholing traffic to a deleted pod IP forever.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a UDP deployment + ClusterIP service (port 9125), 1 replica.
2. From a pod on a different node, send UDP to the ClusterIP from a single long-lived socket (fixed source port) at any steady rate, e.g. 5 pkt/s:
   `while true; do echo ping; sleep 0.2; done | nc -u -p 12345 <ClusterIP> 9125`
3. `kubectl scale deploy/<name> --replicas=0` and wait for the pod to be deleted.
4. On the sender's node, run `conntrack -L -p udp --orig-port-dst 9125`. The entry persists indefinitely (timeout refreshed by every packet), DNAT-ing to the deleted pod IP, even though `iptables-save | grep "has no endpoints"` shows the REJECT rule. `kubeproxy_conntrack_reconciler_deleted_entries_total` does not increase.
5. `kubectl scale --replicas=1`: the entry is deleted on the next sync (counter increments), confirming the reconciler handles the service again as soon as it has an endpoint.

### Anything else we need to know?

- The skip was discussed in the #127318 review: the rationale was that the REJECT rule protects services without endpoints. That holds for new flows (REJECT prevents conntrack confi

title: WatchList initEvents uses a different semantic comparing to the old List+Watch approach
body:
### What happened?

When reflector uses List+Watch, it request ANY version by setting RV=0. [Code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0cd4e13c69be9ec44267efeaf9acfd90ef4af5f5/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go#L1126-L1130)
When reflector uses WatchList, it always requests MostRecent version. [Code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0cd4e13c69be9ec44267efeaf9acfd90ef4af5f5/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go#L1135-L1144)

When the apiserver watch cache is temporarily falling behind (due to high load):
1. A controller with old ListWatch approach is more resilient to temporary staleness given it uses RV=0 .
2. A controller with WatchList with MostRecent semantic approach can suffer longer bootstrap time due to multiple attempts and timeouts. 

More details about the 2nd scenario:
1. Controller (e.g. KCM) initialize a WatchList request with MostRecent
2. APIServer queries etcd to get the latest RV=X
3. APIServer times out after waiting 3s and return 429 to client.
4. Controller retries another WatchList request with MostRecent
5. APIServer queries etcd to get the latest RV=Y (Y>X)
6. APIServer may already have X, but can't catch up with Y in 3s, it returns 429 to client
7. This repeats multiple rounds until the watch cache catches up. During this time, the controller can still hold the leadership because the lease update is cheap and always succeeds even when other resource watch cache is falling behind, but makes no progress for a couple minutes.


### What did you expect to happen?

From resilient to temporary staleness perspective, controller initialization using WatchList should not be worse than the old List+Watch behavior.

A few options to consider:
1. WatchList in Reflector use RV=0 instead of RV="". (easiest and matching old behavior)
2. WatchList can wait longer than 3s before giving up
3. Even when watch cache is not up to date, WatchList starts to serve synthetic events immediately from watch cache and dispatch new etcd events that apiserver receives until it catches up with RV=X. Then it sends the bookmark event. The initEvents no longer contain pure synthetic ADD events.
4. Everything is same as option 3 above except that WatchList starts to serve synthetic events from watch cache after waiting for up to 3s.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/138728#issuecomment-4445545871 should be able to reproduce
